title: A Walk That Visits Every Town Once

concept.title: Extend the path by an unvisited neighbour, undo if it gets stuck
body: A **Hamiltonian path** is a walk along the edges of a graph that visits every vertex **exactly once** (it may start and end anywhere). Nobody knows a fast method for large graphs, but for small graphs backtracking works well: start at a vertex, and extend the path by a neighbour that is not on the path yet.

Because the path may start anywhere, the search is run from **every** vertex. A branch is a dead end when the last vertex has no unvisited neighbour. The worst case is a graph with no path but a large well-connected part, where the search tries every way to walk through that part (at most 9 vertices here, so at most about 10^6 paths).

statement: A graph has `n` towns and `m` two-way roads. Is there a walk that visits every town exactly once, using the roads (it can start and end in any towns)? Print `yes` or `no`.
inputFormat: Each of the next `m` lines has two towns joined by a road.
constraints: 0 <= m <= n * (n - 1) / 2, no repeated roads and no loops

examples.note: The walk 1-2-3-4 visits every town once.

hints: Try every town as the start.
From the last town of the path, go to a neighbour that is not on the path.
If all towns are on the path, the answer is yes; otherwise undo the step and try the next neighbour.

n, m = map(int, input().split())
roads = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(m)]

explanation: From every start, the path is extended by unvisited neighbours; the answer is yes as soon as all `n` towns are on the path, and a dead end is undone and another neighbour tried.
solution.complexity: Time O(n * n!) in the worst case, space O(n).
